# The five evidence sources, and how to read each

A technician standing at a stopped machine has all five of these available and
time to assemble none of them. That gap is the skill.

**MTTR's largest component is usually not the repair.** It is the diagnosis —
working out what is actually wrong. Every minute spent there is a minute the
plant is not producing.

Listed in order of value, which is not the order anyone expects.

---

## 1. Free-text close-out notes — the highest-value input in the plugin

When a technician closes a maintenance work order, they write what they found in
prose:

> *"Bearing was hot, replaced, coupling was misaligned again."*

That sentence contains a diagnosis, a repair, and a recurring root cause that
nobody has acted on. It is written by the person with their hands on the machine,
it is the most honest record in the plant, and **nobody has ever aggregated it.**
It sits in a text field on a work order and is read once, by the person who wrote
it, never again.

### How to mine it

**Search this asset first, then siblings of the same model.** A machine that is
new or has thin history is not a dead end — the same model in the next bay has
been failing in the same ways for years.

**Weight by symptom similarity, then by recency.** A note describing this exact
symptom from two years ago beats a generic note from last month.

**Read what the words actually say, including the throwaway ones.** "Again" is
the single highest-signal word in a close-out note. So are "still," "same as
last time," "temporary fix," and "needs proper repair when we have time." Each
one is a technician telling you this is unresolved.

### Check for templates before citing anything

A CMMS lets a technician pick a stock close-out phrase, and many do. "Spindle
noise reported. Could not reproduce. Monitored." on five machines of three
different makes on the same day is a default, not five observations. Group the
notes by exact text and count the makes and models each group spans (model from
the asset name if the record has no model column; say so). Text shared across
makes is shown, labelled "same text on N assets — not specific to this
machine", and never cited as this asset's evidence. The same failure on
same-model siblings is cited, as a fleet pattern. Do the grouping in code and
print it, so the cited set is the same on every run over the same data.

### Report coverage honestly

Many notes are useless. "Fixed." "Repaired." "OK now." A field that exists is
not a field that says anything.

**State what fraction of the relevant history carried usable notes.** Do not
over-read a terse note into a pattern — per
`../../../shared/absent-is-not-zero.md`, an empty note is not evidence of a
simple repair.

> *"Nine prior work orders on this asset. Four have substantive close-out notes;
> five say only 'repaired' or similar. The pattern below rests on those four."*

---

## 2. The sensor window — read shapes, not thresholds

The historian logs temperature, vibration, pressure and spindle load at high
frequency. Pull a configurable period **before** the failure.

**Look for excursions, trends and step changes — not just threshold breaches.**
This is the whole point. A vibration reading that climbed steadily for six hours
and never once crossed its alarm limit is a bearing failing in plain sight, and a
threshold check reports nothing at all. Three shapes worth naming:

| Shape | Typically means |
|---|---|
| A steady climb | Progressive wear — bearing, tool, belt |
| A step change | Something discrete happened — a part let go, a setting changed, a fixture moved |
| An excursion that recovered | An intermittent fault, which is the hardest kind to catch and the most valuable to have caught |

**Verify the window actually covers the event.** If the export stops an hour
before the failure, say so and **do not reason from adjacent data as if it were
the event.** That is the highest-risk error available here.

**No sensor data at all is very common** — most assets in most plants are not
instrumented. Proceed on the other four sources and say plainly that sensor
evidence was unavailable. This is not a degraded run; it is the normal one.

---

## 3. Maintenance history

What has broken before, what fixed it, what has been replaced recently.

Weight **recency and symptom similarity** together. A part replaced last week is
relevant to a failure this week in a way a five-year-old record is not — both
because it may be the cause and because it may have been installed wrong.

**A new asset with no history falls back to the manual and to sibling assets of
the same model.** State which you used.

---

## 4. Photos — a genuine multimodal advantage

Technicians photograph what they see, and always have. Read them for:

- Visible damage, leaks, scoring, discolouration, wear patterns
- Part numbers on the failed component, which shortens the repair
- Display readings and fault codes on the machine's own panel

**Describe what is visible. Never assert a diagnosis from an unclear image.** A
blurry photo of a dark housing supports nothing, and saying so costs nothing.

> *"The photo shows fluid pooled below the left side of the housing and
> discolouration around the upper bearing cap. I can't tell from this image
> whether the fluid is coolant or hydraulic oil, and that distinction changes
> the diagnosis — worth a look."*

---

## 5. The manufacturer's manual

A PDF sitting in a document library, containing exactly what is needed and never
opened during a breakdown: troubleshooting trees keyed to fault codes,
tolerances, and specified procedures.

Match the fault code the machine is displaying to the manufacturer's own tree,
and **cite the page**. A manufacturer's stated tolerance beats an inference every
time.

# Artifact style — the house look

**Shared across the plugin.** One visual system so every page a skill produces
reads as the same product. Read this before building any HTML artifact; do not
invent a new palette per skill.

**The point is not decoration.** These are operating tools for a plant — a data
quality report, a morning production report, a bad-actor ranking, a cost-basis
sheet. Legible and defensible beats flashy. No hero banners, no marketing
gradients. A shop drawing, not a landing page.

---

## The constraint that shapes everything

**Microsoft 365 is read-only by default.** Write access is an admin opt-in and
Teams has no write path at all. No skill may assume it can post a message or
write a file back into M365.

So every deliverable is produced **in the conversation** and the user places it
themselves. An artifact is a thing they open, read, and save or forward. It is
never something the plugin filed away on their behalf.

**The one exception is the two live dashboards**, Operations and the Quality
Register, which are published to the user's own Claude artifact store and
updated in place, per `live-dashboard.md`. That store is not M365 and not a
system of record. Everything on this page applies to them unchanged.

---

## When to use an artifact, and when not to

Reach for a page when the output is something the user will **refer back to,
print, take into a meeting, or hand to someone else**. A data quality report, a
morning production report, a ranked diagnosis, a scored comparison. Skip it for
a single number or a one-line answer; the chat reply is the deliverable and a
page wrapped around one sentence is noise.

**The artifact is additive, never a replacement.** The user still gets the short
answer in chat. The page is where they go for the full picture.

**Three kinds of output, and only one of them is an artifact:**

| Output | Form | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A report, dashboard, or ranked analysis | HTML artifact, this style | Read at a glance, referred back to |
| A dataset | XLSX workbook, tab per entity | Meant to be filtered, pivoted, and checked |

---

## What this is not

**This is not finite-capacity scheduling.**

Producing an optimal shop schedule is a constraint-optimisation problem. A
language model asked to do it will return a plausible-looking schedule that
quietly violates constraints — and that is **worse than returning nothing**,
because a scheduler who accepts it discovers the violation on the floor, at
which point the report has actively caused a problem it was supposed to report.

So there is a hard line here, and it is drawn deliberately rather than
apologetically.

| Out of scope | In scope |
|---|---|
| Re-optimising the day | One or two specific moves |
| Sequencing every job across every cell | Moving one job, and tracing what that displaces |
| Balancing load across the plant | Naming what still misses its date after the move |
| Anything presented as optimal | Something presented as checked, with the checks listed |

---

## What a proposal must contain

Four parts. A proposal missing any of them is not actionable and should not be
offered.

1. **The move.** Specific: which job, from where, to where — and **the

## Safety: flagged
**Follow your plant's lockout procedure before anyone works on this machine. This is not a safety assessment.**
- **Don't run the spindle, and don't jog it to "listen."** The OEM manual (Sect. 7.4) says not to run a spindle that is making a grinding noise. The operator heard grinding for about 20 minutes before the alarm.
- **Lock out the spindle drive before turning it by hand or inspecting it.** Nobody has hand-turned it yet, so we don't know whether it is seized.
- The spindle drive tripped on overload. The drawbar's Belleville spring stack holds stored energy, so use the drawbar procedure for check (d) below. The bluish colour on the spindle nose means it got very hot.

## The dates don't match what you described
You said "yesterday afternoon," which would be 14 Nov. `event.txt` and the sensor window both put the stoppage at **10 Nov 2026, 15:24**. The production exports only cover **12 Nov**: nothing landed for 13 or 14 Nov. The report is therefore for 12 Nov, not yesterday. ## Event
At 15:24 on 10 Nov, VMC-02 stopped mid-cycle on WO-8120 op 20 (part MB-1880) with the alarm `SPINDLE OVERLOAD / OVERTEMP`. It was still down at 16:10, so it was down for at least 46 min. Nothing in the inputs says what happened after that. **The technician step was skipped**, so the causes below are proposed, not confirmed.

## Ranked causes
**Order of checks (under 30 min, and it separates all three):** (a) chiller fluid level and flow; (b) lock out the drive and turn the spindle by hand; (c) if it turns, measure run-out at the taper; (d) pull the tool holder, look at both tapers, then measure clamp force.

**1. Spindle bearing damage or preload loss, building up over time (confidence: medium, advisory)**
- *Evidence:* vibration went from 1.8 to 11.2 mm/s (6.2×) and temperature from 31.0 to 52.1 °C (+21.1). Both rose at every reading, the climb sped up, and spindle load went from 42% to 71%. The manual links "overtemp with rising vibration" and "grinding noise" to bearings. Two earlier work orders noted the problem and neither led to a follow-up: **MW-118** ("spindle sounded a bit rough at 8k, monitor") and **MW-140** ("vib 2.1 mm/s at 8k (was 1.4 last yr). told sup").
- *First check:* with the drive locked out, turn the spindle by hand. If it feels rough or notchy, that confirms this cause. If it turns, measure run-out at the taper (OEM limit is under 3 µm). Don't run a vibration spectrum, because that needs the spindle running.
- *Expected fix:* rebuild or replace the spindle cartridge, inspect or regrind the taper, and set a new vibration baseline. This is a long-lead job, so get a rebuild quote now.

**2. Chiller low on fluid, so the spindle wasn't cooled properly (confidence: low; more likely a contributor than the sole cause)**
- *Evidence:* **MW-160** ("spindle hot after long cycle… chiller low on fluid topped up"). The fluid loss was never explained. Against this as the only cause: the manual says a cooling fault shows *normal* vibration, and here vibration rose. The sensor file has no chiller channel. Its coolant pressure stayed at 19.8–20.1 bar, but that is very likely the cutting-coolant line.
- *First check:* chiller level, flow and leaks (about 5 min, no need to touch the spindle).
- *Expected fix:* find the leak and verify flow against the OEM spec, which isn't in the manual excerpt you supplied.

**3. Drawbar clamp force too low, so the tool holder slipped in the taper (confidence: low)**
- *Evidence:* **MW-131** (in May: "found drawbar clamp low, adjusted belleville stack"). An overload alarm and heat colour at the taper fit this. Against it: no tool pull-out marks were reported, the chips looked normal, and the pattern looks like bearing wear.

- *Expected fix:* replace the Belleville stack instead of adjusting it again.
